title: How we can beat China
gist: Smith recalibrates his Biden-era Cold War 2 playbook (allied economic bloc plus deterrence, a Kennan-style containment) because Trump-era US internal division and damaged alliances make it unworkable during China's window of peak relative power. He redefines 'beating China' as helping other nations resist Chinese domination and hints China may beat itself; the rest of the post is paywalled.

insights.claim: Smith's earlier Cold War 2 strategy was an updated containment: build economic power within a US-led allied bloc, maintain military deterrence, and wait for China's internal contradictions to remove the threat, as Kennan's Long Telegram strategy did against the USSR over 45 years.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames US-China rivalry as a multi-decade structural contest rather than a short-cycle trade dispute.

insights.claim: Containing China is harder than containing the USSR because China is much bigger, has a better economic model, and is far more globally integrated.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Decoupling costs and supply-chain dependence on China are structurally higher than in Cold War 1.
insights.locator: That strategy was always going to be harder

insights.claim: The allied-scale approach promoted by Rush Doshi and Kurt Campbell aims to build a bloc of allies large enough to overmatch China's manufacturing juggernaut through tighter economic integration.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Friend-shoring and allied industrial policy remain the expert-consensus blueprint; watch for signs of revival.
insights.locator: The strategy I recommended was much tighter

themes.theme: US division breaks the alliance strategy

insights.claim: Smith now believes the allied-bloc strategy probably won't work because the US is too internally divided for far-sighted international competition, with Americans caring more about fighting each other than China.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Lowers the probability of coordinated Western economic pressure on China; China-exposure risk from allied action is smaller than hawks assume.
insights.quote: Americans care more about fighting other Americans than about fighting the Chinese

insights.claim: Trump has degraded or torn up key US alliances, especially with Europe, making the Cold War 2 strategy impossible to prosecute.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Transatlantic fragmentation weakens joint export controls and tariff coordination on China.
insights.locator: Donald Trump's presidency is an outgrowth

insights.claim: Doshi and Campbell argue US alliances could be reconstituted, but Smith expects overcoming US divisions to take decades, exactly the window when China will be at peak relative power, so the chance has largely been missed.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect China's relative power to peak without an effective allied counterweight over the coming decades.
insights.locator: This doesn't mean America's alliance system

insights.claim: Smith expects the GOP not to revert to Reaganism after Trump and Democrats to have only marginal success undoing Trump's geopolitical shifts.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: US foreign-policy illiberalism and alliance unreliability should be treated as persistent, not a one-term anomaly.
insights.locator: And of course Democrats will try

insights.claim: Smith argues Trump has forfeited America's moral superiority claim over China through invasion threats, an immigrant-detention 'gulag archipelago', and 'civilizational' foreign policy, so more US power no longer implies a more liberal world.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Third countries have less reason to align with the US, weakening US leverage in trade and security negotiations.
insights.quote: Trump has thus forfeited America’s claim to moral superiority over China.
insights.locator: But the election of Trump changes

insights.claim: Smith redefines 'beating China' as keeping China from dominating other countries such as Japan, India, the Philippines and Korea, not collapsing China or impoverishing its people, with Europe and Japan as remaining carriers of liberalism.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Points to middle powers (Japan, India, Europe) as the key actors in resisting China, relevant to regional defense and industrial-policy spending.

insights.claim: The post's teaser suggests the new path is to let China defeat itself, noting that many hegemons eventually beat themselves; the full argument is behind a paywall.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Implies a bet on China's internal weaknesses rather than external pressure; full reasoning not available in this text.
insights.quote: The trick is to let them beat themselves.
